title: Bioimpedance meets biomechanics: Wearable electrical impedance myography encodes fascicle and activation dynamics
abstract: Modern assistive robotic control demands parallel advancements in wearable, noninvasive sensing. Electrical impedance myography (EIM)—a noninvasive, wearable technology for dynamically measuring tissue electrical impedance properties—is a promising but poorly established solution for quantifying muscle force and fatigue, given that prior approaches have relied on black-box algorithms when attempting to relate EIM to muscle physiology or have extrapolated relationships between EIM and muscle force from singular, isolated movements. Here, we elucidate direct relationships between EIM and muscle kinematics and kinetics during functional movement using biomechanical principles and traditional measures of joint torque, muscle architecture, and activation. Dual-frequency EIM measurements of the medial gastrocnemius of 10 participants were collected and compared against dynamometer, B-mode ultrasound, and electromyography measurements. Participants performed multiple categories of dynamic movements spanning constrained isometric, self-selected isometric, concentric, and eccentric contractions at multiple force levels, joint angles, and angular velocities. EIM correlated to joint torque only for specific conditions, whereas EIM correlated with muscle length change dynamics across all movements. Mixed-effects modeling and sequential feature analysis showed fascicle length and muscle activation as primary drivers of EIM variance. Last, dual-frequency EIM combined with principal components analysis reliably captured changes in fascicle length and activation during walking. These findings validate EIM as a robust, real-time biomechanical tool for sensing muscle kinematics and neuromuscular activity during functional movement, expanding its use in assistive robotic control and injury prevention.

title: Stabilizing telerobotic endobronchial imaging and interventions in breathing lungs with a helical brace
abstract: Physiological motion in dynamic luminal organs, such as respiration-induced lung displacement, compromises the stability of tool-tissue interaction during telerobotic endoluminal imaging and interventions. However, existing devices for stabilizing the distal end of a catheter or endoscope face critical limitations: Rigid shape-locking mechanisms risk pressure-induced trauma, electrical hazard, and thermal injury, whereas balloon-based designs obstruct luminal patency. Moreover, they lack sufficient adjustable-diameter range for anatomies such as the bronchial tree. In this work, we present a reconfigurable helical brace that overcomes these challenges. Constructed of rotationally stacking tubular modules of asymmetric stiffness, the helical brace achieved up to almost 10 times diameter tunability (3.0 to 29.3 millimeters), enabling adaptive anchoring across diverse bronchial diameters. The established brace in a dynamic bronchus phantom reduced respiration-induced catheter displacement by about 96.0% while preserving more than 97.4% luminal flow conductance. Ex vivo and in vivo bronchial studies confirmed safety under prolonged radial loading, with no notable surface trauma or deep tissue injury observed. We demonstrate a helically braced telerobotic manipulator that can operate with submillimeter control accuracy in dynamic environments, enabling targeted transbronchial needle interventions in live porcine models, including drug delivery, bronchus puncture, and fluid aspiration. In addition, in vivo studies on porcine lungs showed that the brace-aided telerobotic catheter enhances the stability of optical coherence tomography imaging, effectively achieving respiratory motion-free conditions. This patency-preserving brace enhances stabilization without compromising physiological function and safety, ensuring accurate telerobotic operations in dynamic luminal environments.

title: AI-driven actuation-compatible tracking for closed-loop navigation of miniature robots in vivo
abstract: Miniature wireless magnetic robots (MWMRs) hold immense potential for minimally invasive interventions. Real-time tracking of MWMRs is essential for precise in vivo navigation but remains challenging. Tracking MWMRs via their emitted magnetic signals offers a viable solution, yet it has been limited to centimeter-scale robots because isolating weak MWMR signals from overwhelming actuation-induced interference becomes increasingly difficult with miniaturization. Here, we present an artificial intelligence (AI)–driven tracking system to overcome these challenges, enabling precise localization of millimeter-scale MWMRs in the presence of actuation fields. Our approach integrates a sensor array design with a transformer to accurately model and filter the interference, followed by a spatiotemporal transformer that interprets the extracted MWMR signals over a short time window to corresponding three-dimensional coordinates. Our system has been validated in a range of in vitro and in vivo experiments, demonstrating its applicability to closed-loop navigation of MWMRs in unshielded clinical settings.

title: ALBATROSS: A bioinspired, aerially deployable, autonomous sailing sensor platform
abstract: Rapid deployment of autonomous sensor platforms in remote aquatic areas remains a challenge for environmental monitoring, disaster response, and ocean science. We present ALBATROSS (Airborne Lander with Buoyant AuToROtating Sailing Sensor), a hybrid bioinspired robot that passively autorotates for soft water landing and transitions into a wind-driven sailboat. Its dual-function rigid wingsails, acting as both sails and autorotating wings, enable efficient descent and propulsion. A freely rotating main sail, controlled by a tail rudder, and a directly actuated front sail enhance thrust and aerodynamic stability. A biomimetic caudal fin–inspired rudder enables propulsion during low-wind conditions and agile maneuvering in challenging upwind tacking. We empirically evaluated different wingsail airfoils through wind tunnel testing and optimized rudder design through hydrodynamic modeling, material selection, and speed-power efficiency analysis across different sizes and stiffnesses. Field experiments validate aerial deployment from 150 meters, autorotating descent, passive self-righting, and successful waypoint navigation using both rule-based control and a reinforcement learning approach. By integrating minimal actuation, bioinspired structures, and passive dynamics across aerial and marine operating regimes, this work extracts generalizable design principles for lightweight, aerially deployable sailing robots capable of robust, energy-efficient marine sensing.

title: Takeoff of an all-polymer micro aerial flying robot
abstract: Flying insects are agile and can withstand impacts and compression because of their low inertia and resilient wings, exoskeletons, and muscles. These capabilities inspire the development of micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) for surveillance, disaster response, and environmental monitoring in confined or hazardous spaces. However, MAVs, especially subgram flapping-wing platforms, remain fragile because they rely on rigid components in their wings, transmissions, or actuators. We report a resilient all-polymer flying robot weighing 185 milligrams, powered by an electrostrictive bending actuator that directly drives cone-shaped compliant wings without a transmission. The actuator achieves a power density of 1600 watts per kilogram and a bending angle of 136° at 110 hertz, enabling the flying robot to achieve a lift-to-weight ratio of 3.0 and a lift-to-power ratio of 8.3 millinewtons per watt at 30 hertz. The robot demonstrates unaided takeoff with an average ascending speed of 40 centimeters per second. Thanks to its compliant and transmission-free structure, the robot can resume flight after being hit by a flyswatter or flattened by heavy loads. The robot design features mechanical simplicity and resilience, promising a paradigm for subgram flight in harsh environments.

title: Taking aerial-aquatic robots beyond biological capabilities
abstract: An air-dropped robot autorotates to the water and sails off, assembling bioinspired parts into a feat nature has not achieved.

title: What if an alien believes our robot videos?
abstract: In Hole in the Sky , an alien discovers the same problems with replicating robots that real-world roboticists have.

title: Fast Feature Field (F 3 ): A general predictive representation of events for robot perception
abstract: This paper develops a mathematical argument and algorithms for building representations of data from event-based cameras that we call Fast Feature Field (F 3 ). We learned this representation by predicting future events from past events and show that it preserves scene structure and motion information. F 3 exploits the sparsity of event data and is robust to noise and variations in event rates. It can be computed efficiently using ideas from multiresolution hash encoding and deep sets, achieving 120 hertz at high-definition (HD) resolution and 440 hertz at video graphics array (VGA) resolution. F 3 represents events in a contiguous spatiotemporal volume as a multichannel image, enabling a range of downstream tasks. We obtained state-of-the-art performance on optical flow estimation, semantic segmentation, and monocular metric depth estimation, on data from three robotic platforms (a car, a quadruped robot, and a flying platform) and across different lighting conditions (daytime and nighttime), environments (indoors, outdoors, urban, and off-road), and dynamic vision sensors (resolutions and event rates). Our implementations can predict these tasks at 25 to 75 hertz at HD resolution.

title: System design of the Ultra Mobility Vehicle: A driving, balancing, and jumping bicycle robot
abstract: Trials cyclists and mountain bike riders can hop, jump, balance, and drive on one or both wheels. This versatility allows them to achieve speed and energy efficiency on smooth terrain and agility over rough terrain. Inspired by these athletes, we present the design and control of a robotic platform, Ultra Mobility Vehicle (UMV), that combines a bicycle and a reaction mass to move dynamically with minimal actuated degrees of freedom. We used a simulation-driven design optimization process to synthesize a spatial linkage topology with a focus on vertical jump height and momentum-based balancing on a single wheel contact. Using a deep reinforcement learning (RL) framework, we demonstrate zero-shot transfer of diverse athletic behaviors, including track stands, jumps, wheelies, rear-wheel hopping, and front flips. This 23.5-kilogram robot is capable of high speeds ( v max = 8 meters per second) and jumping on and over large obstacles (1-meter tall or 130% of the robot’s nominal height).

title: MonoRace: Robust monocular AI for champion-level drone racing
authors: Guido C. H. E. de Croon
abstract: Autonomous drone racing represents a major frontier in robotics research. It requires an artificial intelligence (AI) that can run onboard lightweight flying robots under tight resource and time constraints while pushing the physical system to its limits. The state of the art in this area consists of a system with a stereo camera and an inertial measurement unit (IMU) that beat human drone-racing champions in a controlled indoor environment. Here, we present MonoRace, an onboard drone-racing approach that generalizes to a competition environment without any external motion tracking system, using only a monocular rolling-shutter camera and an IMU. The approach features robust state estimation that combines neural network–based gate segmentation with a drone model. Moreover, it includes an offline optimization procedure that leverages the known geometry of gates to refine any state estimation parameter. This offline optimization is based purely on onboard flight data and is important for fine-tuning the extrinsic camera calibration parameters. Furthermore, the guidance and control are performed by a neural network that forgoes inner-loop controllers by directly sending motor commands. This small network runs on the flight controller at 500 hertz. The proposed approach won the Abu Dhabi Autonomous Drone Racing Competition 2025, outperforming all competing autonomous drone race teams and three world champion human pilots in a direct knockout tournament. It reached speeds up to 100 kilometers per hour on the competition track and successfully coped with problems such as camera interference and IMU saturation.

title: Hearing the shape of an arena with spectral swarm robotics
abstract: Swarm robotics relies on robots with minimal sensing and computation that achieve self-organization at the level of the collective to address a variety of tasks. Yet, swarm robotics still struggles with global tasks that require understanding the broader spatial context in which robots operate, such as identifying the shape of the arena in which they are embedded. Here, we introduce spectral swarm robotics, a framework in which robots recover global spectral descriptors of the swarm’s geometric structure through strictly local interactions. To do so, robots emulate diffusion to locally estimate Laplacian spectral invariants, quantities normally obtained only through centralized computation. These spectral values serve as compact descriptors of the environment. In the present proof of concept, robots estimated the second Laplacian eigenvalue, λ 2 , and used it to classify arenas from a predefined set of shapes with distinct spectral signatures. We show that estimating a single eigenvalue is sufficient for one-shot classification among selected confined environments with distinct spectral signatures. We uncovered a scaling law linking swarm size (a global parameter) and interaction radius (a local parameter) that ensures robust estimation. We validated the approach experimentally on two distinct hardware platforms, Kilobots and Pogobots, achieving reliable classification of arena shapes under realistic noise and sparse connectivity conditions. Last, we discuss how locally recovering Laplacian spectral invariants opens avenues for swarm robotics in settings where producing efficient collective behaviors strongly depends on the global structure of the swarm.

title: Structural bias enables reliable sim-to-real transfer in reinforcement learning for robot swarms
abstract: Reinforcement learning offers a powerful framework for automatically generating control policies for robot swarms, yet its application to physical multirobot systems has been limited by the simulation-to-reality gap. Despite substantial advances in multiagent reinforcement learning, systematic demonstrations of gradient-based sim-to-real transfer to physical robot swarms remain scarce. Most work remains confined to simulation, and the few real-robot demonstrations lack evaluation across multiple runs and tasks. We show that this barrier can be overcome by embedding structural constraints into policy learning. We introduce attention-based counterfactual policy gradients for behavior selection in robot swarms (SwarmACB), a multiagent actor-critic method in which robots arbitrate among predefined behavior modules—reactive sensorimotor routines such as phototaxis or aggregation—rather than learning low-level motor commands. This architectural choice reduces the variance of learned solutions, which we argue mitigates overfitting to simulation artifacts. Through systematic evaluation on five collective missions using 20 physical e-puck robots (250 real-robot runs), we demonstrate that SwarmACB transfers successfully from simulation to reality, substantially outperforming continuous-action baselines. By progressively constraining policy architecture, perception, and model capacity, we show that smaller, structured policies transfer more reliably than large, unconstrained ones. These findings challenge the assumption that scale is necessary for successful transfer, suggesting instead that principled structural design enables reinforcement learning to produce control software for robot swarms that is both learned automatically and directly deployable in the physical world.

title: Reducing energy and air consumption in scuba diving with underwater exoskeletons
abstract: Assisting underwater locomotion with exoskeletons could reduce energy and air consumption during scuba diving.

title: Bioinspired soft enteroscopic robot for intestinal locomotion, steering, and intervention
abstract: Diagnosing and treating small intestinal disorders such as bleeding, inflammatory bowel disease, and tumors present challenges because of limited access to this anatomical compartment. We present BIOSENTER, a bioinspired soft enteroscopic robot for deep procedures in the small intestine that addresses locomotion, steering, and intervention constraints of existing soft robotic systems. BIOSENTER features a hollow cylinder architecture comprising a linearly deformable soft pneumatic actuator as the body, two radially expandable soft pneumatic actuators wrapped with kirigami sleeves as the head and tail, a central hollow channel for accessory endoscopic tools, and a control box for navigation. Inspired by snake locomotion, the robotic body incorporates a fiber-reinforced actuator with four embedded inflatable chambers, enabling steering and axial expansion. The dynamic kirigami sleeves generate an anchoring force of ∼1.5 newtons on intestinal mucosa while requiring substantially less radial expansion than the corresponding nonkirigami configuration. A reinforced central channel supports tool passage for diagnostic and therapeutic interventions. The control box enables locomotion and steering at autonomous speeds of ∼100 millimeters per minute in vitro and ∼43 millimeters per minute in tissue-covered tubing. BIOSENTER successfully navigated the collapsed, tortuous small intestine for 2 meters in 11 minutes, with gentle forward pushing forces of 2.2 to 6.4 newtons in pig studies. In vivo pig studies demonstrated technical feasibility of tissue biopsy, localized fluid delivery as a model for future drug administration, and real-time visualization of the deep intestine, without macroscopic overdistention or visible tissue damage under the tested conditions.

title: The Mars 2020 OnBoard Planner: Increasing autonomy mission productivity of the Perseverance rover
abstract: Operators of planetary rovers, under strict energy and thermal constraints, face substantial challenges in maintaining high levels of rover productivity because of conservative ground-based planning and long communication latencies. In October 2023, to overcome these limits and increase science return, the Mars 2020 mission deployed OnBoard Planner into Perseverance rover operations. OnBoard Planner uses artificial intelligence constraint–based search to dynamically construct and modify activity schedules on board, adapting to real-time changes in rover state and martian environmental conditions. By replacing conservative ground predictions with real-time resource tracking, the system dynamically adjusts heating durations, reclaims unused schedule margin, and inserts opportunistic activities when extra resources become available. Here, we report on OnBoard Planner’s performance on Mars across more than 2 years of surface operations. The results demonstrate that OnBoard Planner increased discretionary rover activity by 10.5% overall while also improving the thermal and temporal conditions for certain types of scientific observations. Furthermore, the system achieved these productivity gains without increasing ground operations timelines. These findings are part of why OnBoard Planner has successfully become a standard part of Mars 2020 operations and demonstrate how dynamic onboard autonomy can enable resource-efficient operations for complex robotic systems in deep-space environments.

title: Robot autonomous agency by any other name
abstract: The humorous new science fiction novel Valet: A Novel philosophizes about robots gaining free will, but in real life, they may already have it.
